speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: Good evening and welcome to this second of three presidential debates between the major candidates for president of the US.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: The candidates are the Republican nominee, President George Bush, the independent Ross Perot and Governor Bill Clinton, the Democratic nominee.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: My name is Carole Simpson, and I will be the moderator for tonight’s 90-minute debate, which is coming to you from the campus of the University of Richmond in Richmond, Virginia.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: Now, tonight’s program is unlike any other presidential debate in history.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: We’re making history now and it’s pretty exciting.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: An independent polling firm has selected an audience of 209 uncommitted voters from this area.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: The candidates will be asked questions by these voters on a topic of their choosing — anything they want to ask about.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: My job as moderator is to, you know, take care of the questioning, ask questions myself if I think there needs to be continuity and balance, and sometimes I might ask the candidates to respond to what another candidate may have said.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: Now, the format has been agreed to by representatives of both the Republican and Democratic campaigns, and there is no subject matter that is restricted.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: Anything goes.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: We can ask anything.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: After the debate, the candidates will have an opportunity to make a closing statement.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: So, President Bush, I think you said it earlier — let’s get it on.

speaker: CAROLE SIMPSON
text: PRESIDENT GEORGE BUSH: Let’s go.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: And I think the first question is over here.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Yes.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: I’d like to direct my question to Mr.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Perot.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: What will you do as president to open foreign markets to fair competition from American business and to stop unfair competition here at home from foreign countries so that we can bring jobs back to the US?

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: That’s right at the top of my agenda.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: We’ve shipped millions of jobs overseas and we have a strange situation because we have a process in Washington where after you’ve served for a while you cash in, become a foreign lobbyist, make $30,000 a month, then take a leave, work on presidential campaigns, make sure you’ve got good contacts and then go back out.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: Now, if you just want to get down to brass tacks, first thing you ought to do is get all these folks who’ve got these 1-way trade agreements that we’ve negotiated over the years and say fellas, we’ll take the same deal we gave you.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: And they’ll gridlock right at that point because for example, we’ve got international competitors who simply could not unload their cars off the ships if they had to comply — you see, if it was a 2-way street, just couldn’t do it.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: We have got to stop sending jobs overseas.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: To those of you in the audience who are business people: pretty simple.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: If you’re paying $12, $13, $14 an hour for a factory worker, and you can move your factory south of the border, pay $1 an hour for labor, hire a young — let’s assume you’ve been in business for a long time.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: You’ve got a mature workforce.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: Pay $1 an hour for your labor, have no health care — that’s the most expensive single element in making the car.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: Have no environmental controls, no pollution controls and no retirement.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: And you don’t care about anything but making money.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: There will be a job-sucking sound going south.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: If the people send me to Washington the first thing I’ll do is study that 2000-page agreement and make sure it’s a 2-way street.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: One last point here.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: I decided I was dumb and didn’t understand it so I called a “Who’s Who” of the folks that have been around it, and I said why won’t everybody go south; they said it will be disruptive; I said for how long.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: I finally got ’em for 12 to 15 years.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: And I said, well, how does it stop being disruptive?

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: And that is when their jobs come up from a dollar an hour to $6 an hour, and ours go down to $6 an hour; then it’s leveled again, but in the meantime you’ve wrecked the country with these kind of deals.

speaker: ROSS PEROT
text: We got to cut it out.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you, Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: I see that the president has stood up, so he must have something to say about this.

speaker: BUSH
text: Carole, the thing that saved us in this global economic slowdown has been our exports, and what I’m trying to do is increase our exports.

speaker: BUSH
text: And if indeed all the jobs were going to move south because there are lower wages, there are lower wages now and they haven’t done that.

speaker: BUSH
text: And so I have just negotiated with the president of Mexico the North American Free Trade Agreement — and the prime minister of Canada, I might add — and I want to have more of these free trade agreements, because export jobs are increasing far faster than any jobs that may have moved overseas.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s a scare tactic, because it’s not that many.

speaker: BUSH
text: But any one that’s here, we want to have more jobs here.

speaker: BUSH
text: And the way to do that is to increase our exports.

speaker: BUSH
text: Some believe in protection.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t; I believe in free and fair trade, and that’s the thing that saved us.

speaker: BUSH
text: So I will keep on as president trying to get a successful conclusion to the GATT Round, the big Uruguay Round of trade which will really open up markets for our agriculture particularly.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want to continue to work after we get this NAFTA agreement ratified this coming year.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want to get one with Eastern Europe; I want to get one with Chile.

speaker: BUSH
text: And free and fair trade is the answer, not protection.

speaker: BUSH
text: And, as I say, we’ve had tough economic times, and it’s exports that have saved us, exports that have built.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Governor Clinton.

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: I’d like to answer the question, because I’ve actually been a governor for 12 years, so I’ve known a lot of people who have lost their jobs because of jobs moving overseas, and I know a lot of people whose plants have been strengthened by increasing exports.

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: The trick is to expand our export base and to expand trade on terms that are fair to us.

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: It is true that our exports to Mexico, for example, have gone up and our trade deficit has gone down; it’s also true that just today a record high trade deficit was announced with Japan.

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: So what is the answer?

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: Let me just mention three things very quickly.

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: Number one, make sure that other countries are as open to our markets as our markets are to them, and, if they’re not, have measures on the books that don’t take forever and a day to implement.

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: Number two, change the tax code.

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: There are more deductions in the tax code for shutting plants down and moving overseas than there are for modernizing plant and equipment here.

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: Our competitors don’t do that.

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: Emphasize and subsidize modernizing plant and equipment here, not moving plants overseas.

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: Number three, stop the federal government’s program that now gives low-interest loans and job training funds to companies that will actually shut down and move to other countries, but we won’t do the same thing for plants that stay here.

speaker: GOVERNOR CLINTON
text: So more trade but on fair terms — and favor investment in America.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: I think we have a question over here.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: This is for Governor Clinton.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: In the real world, that is, outside of Washington, DC, compensation and achievement are based on goals defined and achieved.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: My question is about the deficit.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Would you define in specific dollar goals how much you would reduce the deficit in each of the 4 years of a Clinton administration and then enter into a legally binding contract with the American people, that if you did not achieve those goals that you would not seek a 2nd term?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Answer yes or no and then comment on your answer, please.

speaker: CLINTON
text: No, and here’s why.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And I’ll tell you exactly why.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Because the deficit now has been building up for 12 years.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ll tell you exactly what I think can be done.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think we can bring it down by 50% in 4 years and grow the economy.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Now, I could get rid of it in 4 years in theory on the books now, but to do it you’d have to raise taxes too much and cut benefits too much to people who need them and it would even make the economy worse.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Perot will tell you, for example, that the expert he hired to analyze his plan says that it will bring the deficit down in 5 years but it will make unemployment bad for 4 more years.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So my view is, sir, you have to increase investment, grow the economy and reduce the deficit by controlling health care costs, prudent reductions in defense, cuts in domestic programs and asking the wealthiest Americans and foreign corporations to pay their fair share of taxes and investing and growing this economy.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I ask everybody to look at my economic ideas and 9 Nobel prize winners and over 500 economists and hundreds of business people, including a lot of Republicans said, this is the way you’ve got to go.

speaker: CLINTON
text: If you don’t grow the economy you can’t get it done.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But I can’t foresee all the things that will happen, and I don’t think a president should be judged solely on the deficit.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Let me also say, we’re having an election today.

speaker: CLINTON
text: You’ll have a shot at me in 4 years and you can vote me right out if you think I’ve done a lousy job and I would welcome you to do that.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: President.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, I’m a little confused here, because I don’t see how you can grow the deficit down by raising people’s taxes.

speaker: BUSH
text: You see, I don’t think the American people are taxed too little.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think they’re taxed too much.

speaker: BUSH
text: I went for one tax increase and when I make a mistake I admit it.

speaker: BUSH
text: I said that wasn’t the right thing to do.

speaker: BUSH
text: Governor Clinton’s program wants to tax more and spend more — $150 billion in new taxes, spend another $220.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t believe that’s the way to do it.

speaker: BUSH
text: Here’s some thing that’ll help.

speaker: BUSH
text: Give us a balanced budget amendment.

speaker: BUSH
text: He always talks about Arkansas having a balanced budget and they do, but he has a balanced budget amendment.

speaker: BUSH
text: Have to do it.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’d like the government to have that.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I think it would discipline not only the Congress, which needs it, but also the executive branch.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’d like to have what 43 governors have — the line item veto, so if the Congress can’t cut, and we’ve got a reckless spending Congress, let the president have a shot at it by wiping out things that are pork barrel or something of that nature.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve proposed another one.

speaker: BUSH
text: Some sophisticates think it may be a little gimmicky.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think it’s good.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s a check- off.

speaker: BUSH
text: It says to you as a taxpayer — say you’re going to pay a tax of 1000 bucks or something.

speaker: BUSH
text: You can check 10% of that if you want to, in the 1 box, and that 10%, $100, or if you’re paying $10,000, whatever it is, $1000, check it off and make the government, make it lower the deficit by that amount.

speaker: BUSH
text: And if the Congress won’t do it, if they can’t get together and negotiate how to do that, then you’d have a sequester across the board.

speaker: BUSH
text: You’d exempt Social Security — I don’t want to tax or touch Social Security.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m the president that said hey, don’t mess with Social Security, and we haven’t.

speaker: BUSH
text: So I believe that we need to control the growth of mandatory spending, back to this gentleman’s question.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s the main growing thing in the budget.

speaker: BUSH
text: The program that the president — two-thirds of the budget, I as president never get to look at, never get to touch.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve got to control that growth to inflation and population increase, but not raise taxes on the American people now.

speaker: BUSH
text: I just don’t believe that would stimulate any kind of growth at all.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: How about you, Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot?

speaker: PEROT
text: Well, we’re $4 trillion in debt.

speaker: PEROT
text: We’re going into debt an additional $1 billion, little more than $1 billion every working day of the year.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, the thing I love about it — I’m just a businessman.

speaker: PEROT
text: I was down in Texas taking care of business, tending to my family.

speaker: PEROT
text: This situation got so bad that I decided I’d better get into it.

speaker: PEROT
text: The American people asked me to get into it.

speaker: PEROT
text: But I just find it fascinating that while we sit here tonight we will go into debt an additional $50 million in an hour and a half.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, it’s not the Republicans’ fault, of course, and it’s not the Democrats’ fault.

speaker: PEROT
text: And what I’m looking for is who did it?

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, they’re the 2 folks involved so maybe if you put them together, they did it.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, the facts are we have to fix it.

speaker: PEROT
text: I’m here tonight for these young people up here in the balcony from this college.

speaker: PEROT
text: When I was a young man, when I got out of the Navy I had multiple job offers.

speaker: PEROT
text: Young people with high grades can’t get a job.

speaker: PEROT
text: People — the 18- to 24-year-old high school graduates 10 years ago were making more than they are now.

speaker: PEROT
text: In other words, we were down to 18% of them were making — 18- to 24-year- olds were making less than $12,000.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now that’s up to 40%.

speaker: PEROT
text: And what’s happened in the meantime?

speaker: PEROT
text: The dollar’s gone through the floor.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, whose fault is that?

speaker: PEROT
text: Not the Democrats.

speaker: PEROT
text: Not the Republicans.

speaker: PEROT
text: Somewhere out there there’s an extraterrestrial that’s doing this to us, I guess.

speaker: PEROT
text: And everybody says they take responsibility.

speaker: PEROT
text: Somebody somewhere has to take responsibility for this.

speaker: PEROT
text: Put it to you bluntly, American people.

speaker: PEROT
text: If you want me to be your president, we’re going to face our problems.

speaker: PEROT
text: Weâ€™ll deal with our problems, weâ€™ll solve our problems.

speaker: PEROT
text: We’ll down our debt.

speaker: PEROT
text: We’ll pass on the American dream to our children, and I will not leave our children a situation that they have today.

speaker: PEROT
text: When I was a boy it took 2 generations to double the standard of living.

speaker: PEROT
text: Today it will take 12 generations.

speaker: PEROT
text: Our children will not see the American dream because of this debt that somebody somewhere dropped on us.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: You’re all wonderful speakers, and I know you have lots more to add, but I’ve talked to this audience, and they have lots of questions on other topics.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Can we move to another topic, please?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: We have one up here, I think.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Yes, I’d like to address all the candidates with this question.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: The amount of time the candidates have spent in this campaign trashing their opponents’ character and their programs is depressingly large.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Why can’t your discussions and proposals reflect the genuine complexity and the difficulty of the issues to try to build a consensus around the best aspects of all proposals?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Who wants to take that one?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot, you have an answer for everything, don’t you?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Go right ahead, sir.

speaker: PEROT
text: No, I don’t have an answer for everything.

speaker: PEROT
text: As you all know, I’ve been buying 30-minute segments to talk about issues.

speaker: PEROT
text: And tomorrow night on NBC, from 10:30 to 11 Eastern, we’re going to talk about how you pay the debt down, so we’re going to come right down to that one.

speaker: PEROT
text: We’ll be on again Saturday night, 8 to 9 o’clock on ABC.

speaker: PEROT
text: So the point is —

speaker: BUSH
text: Like Jerry Brown, the 800 number.

speaker: PEROT
text: — I couldn’t agree with you more, couldn’t agree with you more.

speaker: PEROT
text: And I have said again and again and again let’s get off mud wrestling, let’s get off personalities and let’s talk about jobs, health care, crime, the things that concern the American people.

speaker: PEROT
text: I’m spending my money — not PAC money, not foreign money, my money — to take this message to the people.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you, Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: So that seems directed; he would say it’s you gentlemen that have been doing that.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Clinton, Governor Clinton — oh, President Bush, how would you like to respond?

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, in the first place, I believe that character is a part of being president.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think you have to look at it.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think that has to be a part of a candidate for president or being president.

speaker: BUSH
text: In terms of programs, I’ve submitted, what, 4 different budgets to the US Congress in great detail.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s so heavy they’d give you a broken back.

speaker: BUSH
text: And everything in there says what I am for.

speaker: BUSH
text: Now I’ve come out with a new agenda for America’s renewal, a plan that I believe really will help stimulate the growth of this economy.

speaker: BUSH
text: My record on world affairs is pretty well known because I’ve been president for 4 years, so I feel I’ve been talking issues.

speaker: BUSH
text: You know, nobody likes who shot John, but I think the first negative campaign run in this election was by Governor Clinton, and I’m not going to sit there and be a punching bag; I’m going to stand up and say, hey, listen, here’s my side of it.

speaker: BUSH
text: But character is an important part of the equation.

speaker: BUSH
text: The other night Governor Clinton raised my — I don’t know if you saw the debate the other night.

speaker: BUSH
text: You did — suffered through that?

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, he raised the question of my father — it was a good line, well rehearsed and well delivered.

speaker: BUSH
text: But he raised the question of my father and said, well, your father, Prescott Bush, was against McCarthy, you should be ashamed of yourself, McCarthyism.

speaker: BUSH
text: I remember something my dad told me — I was 18 years old going to Penn Station to go on into the Navy, and he said write your mother — which I faithfully did; he said serve your country — my father was an honor, duty and country man; and he said tell the truth.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I’ve tried to do that in public life, all through it.

speaker: BUSH
text: That says something about character.

speaker: BUSH
text: My argument with Governor Clinton — you can call it mud wrestling, but I think it’s fair to put it in focus is — I am deeply troubled by someone who demonstrates and organizes demonstration in a foreign land when his country’s at war.

speaker: BUSH
text: Probably a lot of kids here disagree with me.

speaker: BUSH
text: But that’s what I feel.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what I feel passionately about.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m thinking of Ross Perot’s running mate sitting in the jail.

speaker: BUSH
text: How would he feel about it?

speaker: BUSH
text: But maybe that’s generational.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t know.

speaker: BUSH
text: But the big argument I have with the governor on this is this taking different positions on different issues — trying to be one thing to one person here that’s opposing the NAFTA agreement and then for it — what we call waffling.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I do think that you can’t turn the White House into the Waffle House.

speaker: BUSH
text: You’ve got to say what you’re for and you’ve got to —

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: President, I’m getting time cues and with all due respect —

speaker: BUSH
text: Excuse me.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t want to —

speaker: SIMPSON
text: I’m sorry.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t want to —

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Governor Clinton.

speaker: BUSH
text: I get wound up because I feel strongly —

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Yes, you do.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Let me say first of all to you that I believe so strongly in the question you asked that I suggested this format tonight.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I started doing these formats a year ago in New Hampshire and I found that we had huge crowds because all I did was let people ask questions and I tried to give very specific answers.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I also had a program starting last year.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ve been disturbed by the tone and the tenor of this campaign.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Thank goodness the networks have a fact check so I don’t have to just go blue in the face anymore.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Bush said once again I was going to have $150 billion tax increase.

speaker: CLINTON
text: When Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Quayle said that all the networks said, that’s not true.

speaker: CLINTON
text: He’s got over $100 billion of tax cuts and incentives.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So I’m not going to take up your time tonight, but let me just say this.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We’ll have a debate in 4 days and we can talk about this character thing again.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But the Washington Post ran a long editorial today saying they couldn’t believe Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Bush was making character an issue and they said he was the greatest quote “political chameleon” for changing his positions of all times.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Now, I don’t want to get into that —

speaker: BUSH
text: Please don’t get into the Washington Post.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Wait a minute.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Let’s don’t — you don’t have to believe it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Here’s my point.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’m not interested in his character.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I want to change the character of the presidency.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And I’m interested in what we can trust him to do and what you can trust me to do and what you can trust Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Perot to do for the next 4 years.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So I think you’re right and I hope the rest of the night belongs to you.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: May I — I talked to this audience before you gentlemen came and I asked them about how they felt about the tenor of the campaign.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Would you like to let them know what you thought about that, when I said are you pleased with how the campaign’s been going?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Who wants to say why you don’t like the way the campaign is going?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: We have a gentleman back here.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: And forgive the notes here but I’m shy on camera.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: The focus of my work as a domestic mediator is meeting the needs of the children that I work with, by way of their parents, and not the wants of their parents.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: And I ask the three of you, how can we, as symbolically the children of the future president, expect the two of you, the three of you to meet our needs, the needs in housing and in crime and you name it, as opposed to the wants of your political spin doctors and your political parties?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: So your question is?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Can we focus on the issues and not the personalities and the mud?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: I think there’s a need, if we could take a poll here with the folks from Gallup perhaps, I think there’s a real need here to focus at this point on the needs.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: How do you respond?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: How do you gentlemen respond to —

speaker: CLINTON
text: I agree with him.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let’s do it.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: President Bush?

speaker: BUSH
text: Let’s do it.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let’s talk about programs for children.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Could we cross our hearts?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: It sounds silly here but could we make a commitment?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: You know, we’re not under oath at this point but could you make a commitment to the citizens of the US to meet our needs, and we have many, and not yours again?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: I repeat that.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: It’s a real need, I think, that we all have.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think it depends how you define it.

speaker: BUSH
text: I mean, I think in general, let’s talk about these issues.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let’s talk about the programs.

speaker: BUSH
text: But in the presidency, a lot goes into it.

speaker: BUSH
text: Caring goes into it.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s not particularly specific.

speaker: BUSH
text: Strength goes into it.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s not specific.

speaker: BUSH
text: Standing up against aggression.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s not specific in terms of a program.

speaker: BUSH
text: This is what a president has to do.

speaker: BUSH
text: So in principle, though, I’ll take your point and think we ought to discuss child care or whatever else it is.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: And you, too?

speaker: CLINTON
text: Ross had his hand up.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Yes.

speaker: PEROT
text: Just no hedges, no ifs, ands and buts.

speaker: PEROT
text: I’ll take the pledge because I know the American people want to talk about issues and not tabloid journalism.

speaker: PEROT
text: So I’ll take the pledge and will stay on the issues.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, just for the record, I don’t have any spin doctors.

speaker: PEROT
text: I don’t have any speechwriters.

speaker: PEROT
text: Probably shows.

speaker: PEROT
text: I make those charts you see on television.

speaker: PEROT
text: But you don’t have to wonder if it’s me talking.

speaker: PEROT
text: See, what you see is what you get and if you don’t like it, you got two other choices, right?

speaker: CLINTON
text: Wait a minute.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I want to say just one thing now, Ross, in fairness.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The ideas I express are mine.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ve worked on these things for 12 years and I’m the only person up here who hasn’t been part of Washington in any way for the last 20 years.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So I don’t want the implication to be that somehow everything we say is just cooked up and put in our head by somebody else.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I worked 12 years very hard as a governor on the real problems of real people.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’m just as sick as you are by having to wake up and figure out how to defend myself every day.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I never thought I’d ever be involved in anything like this.

speaker: PEROT
text: May I finish?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Yes, you may finish.

speaker: PEROT
text: Very briefly?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Yes, very briefly.

speaker: PEROT
text: And I don’t have any foreign money in my campaign.

speaker: PEROT
text: I don’t have any foreign lobbyists on leave in my campaign.

speaker: PEROT
text: I don’t have any PAC money in my campaign.

speaker: PEROT
text: I’ve got 5.

speaker: PEROT
text: 5 million hard-working people who put me on the ballot, and I belong to them.

speaker: PEROT
text: And they’re interested in what you’re interested in.

speaker: PEROT
text: I take the pledge.

speaker: PEROT
text: I’ve already taken the pledge on cutting the deficit in half.

speaker: PEROT
text: I never got to say that.

speaker: PEROT
text: There’s a great young group, Lead or Leave, college students, young people, who don’t want us to spend their money.

speaker: PEROT
text: I took the pledge we’d cut it out.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: We have a question here.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Yes.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: I would like to get a response from all three gentlemen.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: And the question is, what are your plans to improve the physical infrastructure of this nation, which includes the water system, the sewer system, our transportation systems, etcetera.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Thank you.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: The cities.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Who’s going to fix the cities and how?

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ll be glad to take a shot at it.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Please.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m not sure that — and I can understand if you haven’t seen this, because there’s been a lot of hue and cry.

speaker: BUSH
text: We passed this year the most furthest looking transportation bill in the history of this country since Eisenhower started the interstate highways — $150 billion for improving the infrastructure.

speaker: BUSH
text: That happened when I was president.

speaker: BUSH
text: And so I’m very proud of the way that came about and I think it’s a very, very good beginning.

speaker: BUSH
text: Like Mr.

speaker: BUSH
text: Perot, I am concerned about the deficits and $150 billion is a lot of money, but it’s awful hard to say we’re going to go out and spend more money when we’re trying to get the deficit down.

speaker: BUSH
text: But I would cite that as a major accomplishment.

speaker: BUSH
text: We hear all the negatives.

speaker: BUSH
text: When you’re president you expect this.

speaker: BUSH
text: Everybody’s running against the incumbent.

speaker: BUSH
text: They can do better.

speaker: BUSH
text: Everyone knows that.

speaker: BUSH
text: But here’s something that we can take great pride in because it really does get to what you’re talking about.

speaker: BUSH
text: Our home initiative — our home ownership initiative — HOPE — that passed the Congress is a good start for having people own their own homes instead of living in these deadly tenements.

speaker: BUSH
text: Our enterprise zones, that we hear a lot of lip service about in Congress, would bring jobs into the inner city.

speaker: BUSH
text: There’s a good program.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I need the help of everybody across this country to get it passed in a substantial way by the Congress.

speaker: BUSH
text: When we went out to south central in Los Angeles — some of you may remember the riots there.

speaker: BUSH
text: I went out there.

speaker: BUSH
text: I went to a boys’ club.

speaker: BUSH
text: And everyone of them — the boys’ club leaders, the ministers — all of them were saying pass enterprise zones.

speaker: BUSH
text: We go back to Washington and very difficult to get it through the Congress.

speaker: BUSH
text: But there’s going to be a new Congress.

speaker: BUSH
text: No one likes gridlock.

speaker: BUSH
text: There’s going to be a new Congress because the old one — I don’t want to get this man made at me — but there was a post office scandal and a bank scandal.

speaker: BUSH
text: You’re going to have a lot of new members of Congress.

speaker: BUSH
text: And then you can sit down and say, help me do what we should for the cities.

speaker: BUSH
text: Help me pass these programs.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: President, aren’t you threatening to veto the bill — the urban aid bill — that included enterprise zones?

speaker: BUSH
text: Sure, but the problem is, you get so many things included in a great big bill that you have to look at the overall good.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s the problem with our system.

speaker: BUSH
text: If you had a line item veto you could knock out the pork.

speaker: BUSH
text: You could knock out the tax increases and you could do what the people want, and that’s create enterprise zones.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Governor Clinton, you’re chomping at the bit.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That bill pays for these urban enterprise zones by asking the wealthiest Americans to pay a little more.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And that’s why he wants to veto it, just like he vetoed an earlier bill this year.

speaker: CLINTON
text: This is not mud slinging.

speaker: CLINTON
text: This is fact slinging — a bill earlier this year.

speaker: CLINTON
text: This is facts — that would have given investment tax credits and other incentives to reinvest in our cities, in our country.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But it asked the wealthiest Americans to pay a little more.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Perot wants to do the same thing.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I agree with him.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I mean, we agree with that.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But let me tell you specifically what my plan does.

speaker: CLINTON
text: My plan would dedicate $20 billion a year in each of the next 4 years for investments in new transportation, communications, environmental clean-ups and new technologies for the 21st century.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And we would target it especially in areas that have been either depressed or which have lost a lot of defense related jobs.

speaker: CLINTON
text: There are 200,000 people in California, for example, who have lost their defense related jobs.

speaker: CLINTON
text: They ought to be engaged in making high speed rail.

speaker: CLINTON
text: They ought to be engaged in breaking ground in other technologies, doing waste recycling, clean water technology and things of that kind.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We can create millions of jobs in these new technologies- -more than we’re going to lose in defense — if we target it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But we’re investing a much smaller percentage of our income in the things you just asked about than all of our major competitors, and our wealth growth is going down as a result of it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It’s making the country poorer, which is why I answered the gentleman the way I did before.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We have to both bring down the deficit and get our economy going through these kinds of investments in order to get the kind of wealth and jobs and incomes we need in America.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot, what about your plans for the cities?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: You want to tackle the economy and the deficit first.

speaker: PEROT
text: First you’ve got to have money to pay for these things.

speaker: PEROT
text: So you’ve got to create jobs.

speaker: PEROT
text: There are all kinds of ways to create jobs in the inner city.

speaker: PEROT
text: I’m not a politician, but I think I could go to Washington in a week and get everybody holding hands and get this bill signed because I talk to the Democratic leaders and they want it.

speaker: PEROT
text: I talk to the Republican leaders and they want it.

speaker: PEROT
text: But since they’re bred from childhood to fight with one another rather than get results, you know, I would be glad to drop out and spend a little time and see if we couldn’t build some bridges.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, results is what counts.

speaker: PEROT
text: The president can’t order Congress around.

speaker: PEROT
text: Congress can’t order the president around.

speaker: PEROT
text: That’s not bad for a guy that’s never been there, right?

speaker: PEROT
text: But you have to work together.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, I have talked to the chairmen of the committees that want this.

speaker: PEROT
text: They’re Democrats.

speaker: PEROT
text: The president wants it, but we can’t get it because we sit here in gridlock because it’s a campaign year.

speaker: PEROT
text: We didn’t fund a lot of other things this year, like the savings and loan mess.

speaker: PEROT
text: That’s another story that we’re going to pay a big price for right after the election.

speaker: PEROT
text: The facts are though — the facts are — the American people are hurting.

speaker: PEROT
text: These people are hurting in the inner cities.

speaker: PEROT
text: We’re shipping the quote, “low paying jobs” overseas.

speaker: PEROT
text: What are low paying jobs?

speaker: PEROT
text: Textiles, shoes, things like that that we say are yesterday’s industries.

speaker: PEROT
text: They’re tomorrow’s industries in the inner cities.

speaker: PEROT
text: Let me say in my case, if I’m out of work, I’ll cut grass tomorrow to take care of my family; I’ll be happy to make shoes, I’ll be happy to make clothing, I’ll make sausage.

speaker: PEROT
text: You just give me a job.

speaker: PEROT
text: Put those jobs in the inner cities instead of doing diplomatic deals and shipping them to China where prison labor does the work.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot, everybody thought you won the first debate because you were plain-speaking and you made it sound, oh, so simple.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Well, just do it.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: What makes you think that you’re going to be able to get the Democrats and Republicans together any better than these guys?

speaker: PEROT
text: If you ask me if I could fly a fighter plane or be an astronaut, I can’t.

speaker: PEROT
text: I’ve spent my life creating jobs.

speaker: PEROT
text: That’s something I know how to do.

speaker: PEROT
text: And, very simply, in the inner city, they’re starved — you see, small business is the way to jump start the inner city, not —

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Are you answering my question?

speaker: PEROT
text: You want jobs in the inner city?

speaker: PEROT
text: Do you want jobs in the inner city?

speaker: PEROT
text: Is that your question?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: No, I want you to tell me how you’re going to be able to get the Republicans and Democrats in Congress to work together better than these two gentlemen.

speaker: PEROT
text: Oh, I’m sorry.

speaker: PEROT
text: Well, I’ve listened to both sides, and if they would talk to one another instead of throwing rocks, I think we could get a lot done.

speaker: PEROT
text: And, among other things, I would say, okay, over here in this Senate committee to the chairman who is anxious to get this bill passed, the president who is anxious, I’d say rather than just yelling at one another, why don’t we find out where we’re apart, try to get together, get the bill passed and give the people the benefits and not play party politics right now.

speaker: PEROT
text: And I think the press would follow that so closely that probably they would get it done.

speaker: PEROT
text: That’s the way I would do it.

speaker: PEROT
text: I doubt if they’ll give me the chance, but I will drop everything and go work on it.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Okay, I have a question here.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: My question was originally for Governor Clinton, but I think I would welcome a response from all three candidates.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: As you are aware, crime is rampant in our cities.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: And in the Richmond area — and I’m sure it’s happened elsewhere — 12-year-olds are carrying guns to school.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: And I’m sure when our Founding Fathers wrote the Constitution they did not mean for the right to bear arms to apply to 12-year-olds.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: So I’m asking: Where do you stand on gun control, and what do you plan to do about it?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Governor Clinton?

speaker: CLINTON
text: I support the right to keep and bear arms.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I live in a state where over half the adults have hunting or fishing licenses, or both.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But I believe we have to have some way of checking hand guns before they’re sold, to check the criminal history, the mental health history, and the age of people who are buying them.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Therefore I support the Brady bill which would impose a national waiting period unless and until a state did what only Virginia has done now, which is to automate its records.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Once you automate your records, then you don’t have to have a waiting period, but at least you can check.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I also think we should have frankly restrictions on assault weapons whose only purpose is to kill.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We need to give the police a fighting chance in our urban areas where the gangs are building up.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The third thing I would say — it doesn’t bear directly on gun control, but it’s very important — we need more police on the street.

speaker: CLINTON
text: There is a crime bill which would put more police on the street, which was killed for this session by a filibuster in the Senate, mostly be Republican senators, and I think it’s a shame it didn’t pass, I think it should be made the law — but it had the Brady bill in it, the waiting period.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I also believe that we should offer college scholarships to people who will agree to work them off as police officers, and I think, as we reduce our military forces, we should let people earn military retirement by coming out and working as police officers.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Thirty years ago there were three police officers on the street for every crime; today there are three crimes for every police officer.

speaker: CLINTON
text: In the communities which have had real success putting police officers near schools where kids carry weapons, to get the weapons out of the schools, are on the same blocks, you’ve seen crime go down.

speaker: CLINTON
text: In Houston there’s been a 15- percent drop in the crime rate in the last year because of the work the mayor did there in increasing the police force.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So I know it can work; I’ve seen it happen.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: President Bush?

speaker: BUSH
text: I think you put your finger on a major problem.

speaker: BUSH
text: I talk about strengthening the American family and it’s very hard to strengthen the family if people are scared to walk down to the corner store and, you know, send their kid down to get a loaf of bread.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s very hard.

speaker: BUSH
text: I have been fighting for very strong anti-crime legislation — habeas corpus reform, so you don’t have these endless appeals, so when somebody gets sentenced, hey, this is for real.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve been fighting for changes in the exclusionary rule so if an honest cop stops somebody and makes a technical mistake, the criminal doesn’t go away.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ll probably get into a fight in this room with some but I happen to think that we need stronger death penalties for those that kill police officers.

speaker: BUSH
text: Virginia’s in the lead in this, as Governor Clinton properly said, on this identification system for firearms.

speaker: BUSH
text: I am not for national registration of firearms.

speaker: BUSH
text: Some of the states that have the toughest anti-gun laws have the highest levels of crime.

speaker: BUSH
text: I am for the right, as the governor says- -I’m a sportsman and I don’t think you ought to eliminate all kinds of weapons.

speaker: BUSH
text: But I was not for the bill that he was talking about because it was not tough enough on the criminal.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m very pleased that the Fraternal Order of Police in Little Rock, Arkansas endorsed me because I think they see I’m trying to strengthen the anti-crime legislation.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve got more money going out for local police than any previous administration.

speaker: BUSH
text: So we’ve got to get it under control and there’s one last point I’d make.

speaker: BUSH
text: Drugs.

speaker: BUSH
text: We have got to win our national strategy against drugs, the fight against drugs.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we’re making some progress, doing a little better on interdiction.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re not doing as well amongst the people that get to be habitual drug-users.

speaker: BUSH
text: The good news is, and I think it’s true in Richmond, teenage use is down of cocaine, substantially, 60% in the last couple of years.

speaker: BUSH
text: So we’re making progress but until we get that one done, we’re not going to solve the neighborhood crime problem.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot, there are young black males in America dying at unprecedented rates —

speaker: PEROT
text: I didn’t get to make a comment on this.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Yes, I’m getting to that.

speaker: PEROT
text: Oh, you’re going to let me.

speaker: PEROT
text: Excuse me.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: The fact that homicide is the leading cause of death among young black males 15 to 24 years old.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: What are you going to do to get the guns off the street?

speaker: PEROT
text: On any program, and this includes crime, you’ll find we have all kinds of great plans lying around that never get enacted into law and implemented.

speaker: PEROT
text: I don’t care what it is — competitiveness, health care, crime, you name it.

speaker: PEROT
text: Brady Bill, I agree that it’s a timid step in the right direction but it won’t fix it.

speaker: PEROT
text: So why pass a law that won’t fix it?

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, what it really boils down to is can you live — we become so preoccupied with the rights of the criminal that we’ve forgotten the rights of the innocent.

speaker: PEROT
text: And in our country we have evolved to a point where we’ve put millions of innocent people in jail because you go to the poor neighborhoods and they’ve put bars on their windows and bars on their doors and put themselves in jail to protect the things that they acquired legitimately.

speaker: PEROT
text: That’s where we are.

speaker: PEROT
text: We have got to become more concerned about people who play by the rules and get the balance we require.

speaker: PEROT
text: This is going to take first, building a consensus at grassroots America.

speaker: PEROT
text: Right from the bottom up, the American people have got to say they want it.

speaker: PEROT
text: And at that point, we can pick from a variety of plans and develop new plans.

speaker: PEROT
text: And the way you get things done is bury yourselves in the room with one another, put together the best program, take it to the American people, use the electronic town hall, the kind of thing you’re doing here tonight, build a consensus and then do it and then go on to the next one.

speaker: PEROT
text: But don’t just sit here slow dancing for 4 years doing nothing.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you, Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: We have a question up here.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Please state your position on term limits, and, if you are in favor of them, how will you get them enacted?

speaker: BUSH
text: Any order?

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ll be glad to respond.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you.

speaker: BUSH
text: I strongly support term limits for members of the US Congress.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe it would return the government closer to the people, the way that Ross Perot is talking about.

speaker: BUSH
text: The president’s terms are limited to 2, a total of 8 years.

speaker: BUSH
text: What’s wrong with limiting the terms of members of Congress to 12?

speaker: BUSH
text: Congress has gotten kind of institutionalized.

speaker: BUSH
text: For 38 years one party has controlled the House of Representatives, and the result, a sorry little post office that can’t do anything right and a bank that has more overdrafts than all the Chase Bank and Citibank put together.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve got to do something about it.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I think you get a certain arrogance, bureaucratic arrogance, if people stay there too long.

speaker: BUSH
text: And so I favor, strongly favor, term limits.

speaker: BUSH
text: And how to get them passed?

speaker: BUSH
text: Send us some people that will pass the idea.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I think you will.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think the American people want it now.

speaker: BUSH
text: Every place I go I talk about it, and I think they want it done.

speaker: BUSH
text: Actually, you’d have to have some amendments to the Constitution because of the way the Constitution reads.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Governor Clinton.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I know they’re popular, but I’m against them.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ll tell you why.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I believe, number one, it would pose a real problem for a lot of smaller states in the Congress who have enough trouble now making sure their interests are heard.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Number 2, I think it would increase the influence of unelected staff members in the Congress who have too much influence already.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I want to cut the size of the congressional staffs, but I think you’re going to have too much influence there with people who were never elected, who have lots of expertise.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Number 3, if the people really have a mind to change, they can.

speaker: CLINTON
text: You’re going to have 120 to 150 new members of Congress.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Now, let me tell you what I favor instead.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I favor strict controls on how much you can spend running for Congress, strict limits on political action committees, requirements that people running for Congress appear in open public debates like we’re doing now.

speaker: CLINTON
text: If you did that you could take away the incumbents’ advantage because challengers like me would have a chance to run against incumbents like him for House races and Senate races, and then the voters could make up their own mind without being subject to an unfair fight.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So that’s how I feel about it, and I think if we had the right kind of campaign reform, we’d get the changes you want.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot, would you like to address term limitations?

speaker: PEROT
text: Yes.

speaker: PEROT
text: Let me do first on a personal level.

speaker: PEROT
text: If the American people send me up to do this job, I intend to be there one term.

speaker: PEROT
text: I do not intend to spend one minute of one day thinking about re-election.

speaker: PEROT
text: And as a matter of principle — and my situation is unique, and I understand it — I would take absolutely no compensation; I go as their servant.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, I have set as strong an example as I can, then at that point when we sit down over at Capitol Hill — tomorrow night I’m going to be talking about government reform — it’s a long subject, you wouldn’t let me finish tonight.

speaker: PEROT
text: If you want to hear it, you get it tomorrow night — you’ll hear it tomorrow night.

speaker: PEROT
text: But we have got to reform government.

speaker: PEROT
text: If you put term limits in and don’t reform government, you won’t get the benefits you thought.

speaker: PEROT
text: It takes both.

speaker: PEROT
text: So we need to do the reforms and the term limits.

speaker: PEROT
text: And after we reform it, it won’t be a lifetime career opportunity; good people will go serve and then go back to their homes and not become foreign lobbyists and cash in at 30,000 bucks a month and then take time off to run some president’s campaign.

speaker: PEROT
text: They’re all nice people, they’re just in a bad system.

speaker: PEROT
text: I don’t think there are any villains, but, boy, is the system rotten.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you very much.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: We have a question over here.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: I’d like to ask Governor Clinton, do you attribute the rising costs of health care to the medical profession itself, or do you think the problem lies elsewhere?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: And what specific proposals do you have to tackle this problem?

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ve had more people talk to me about their health care problems I guess than anything else, all across America — you know, people who’ve lost their jobs, lost their businesses, had to give up their jobs because of sick children.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So let me try to answer you in this way.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Let’s start with a premise.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We spend 30% more of our income than any nation on earth on health care, and yet we insure fewer people.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We have 35 million people without any insurance at all — and I see them all the time.

speaker: CLINTON
text: A hundred thousand Americans a month have lost their health insurance just in the last 4 years.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So if you analyze where we’re out of line with other countries, you come up with the following conclusions.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Number one, we spend at least $60 billion a year on insurance, administrative cost, bureaucracy, and government regulation that wouldn’t be spent in any other nation.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So we have to have, in my judgment, a drastic simplification of the basic health insurance policies of this country, be very comprehensive for everybody.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Employers would cover their employees, government would cover the unemployed.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Number 2, I think you have to take on specifically the insurance companies and require them to make some significant change in the way they rate people in the big community pools.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think you have to tell the pharmaceutical companies they can’t keep raising drug prices at three times the rate of inflation.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think you have to take on medical fraud.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think you have to help doctors stop practicing defensive medicine.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ve recommended that our doctors be given a set of national practice guidelines and that if they follow those guidelines that raises the presumption that they didn’t do anything wrong.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think you have to have a system of primary and preventive clinics in our inner cities and our rural areas so people can have access to health care.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The key is to control the cost and maintain the quality.

speaker: CLINTON
text: To do that you need a system of managed competition where all of us are covered in big groups and we can choose our doctors and our hospitals, a wide range, but there is an incentive to control costs.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And I think there has to be — I think Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Perot and I agree on this, there has to be a national commission of health care providers and health care consumers that set ceilings to keep health costs in line with inflation, plus population growth.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Now, let me say, some people say we can’t do this but Hawaii does it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: They cover 98% of their people and their insurance premiums are much cheaper than the rest of America, and so does Rochester, New York.

speaker: CLINTON
text: They now have a plan to cover everybody and their premiums are two-thirds of the rest of the country.

speaker: CLINTON
text: This is very important.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It’s a big human problem and a devastating economic problem for America, and I’m going to send a plan to do this within the first 100 days of my presidency.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It’s terribly important.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Sorry to cut you short but President Bush, health care reform.

speaker: BUSH
text: I just have to say something.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t want to stampede.

speaker: BUSH
text: Ross was very articulate across the country.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t want anybody to stampede to cut the president’s salary off altogether.

speaker: BUSH
text: Barbara’s sitting over here and I — but what I have proposed, 10% cut, downsize the government, and we can get that done.

speaker: BUSH
text: She asked a question, I think, is whether the health care profession was to blame.

speaker: BUSH
text: No.

speaker: BUSH
text: One thing to blame is these malpractice lawsuits.

speaker: BUSH
text: They’re breaking the system.

speaker: BUSH
text: It costs $20-25 billion a year, and I want to see those outrageous claims capped.

speaker: BUSH
text: Doctors don’t dare to deliver babies sometimes because they’re afraid that somebody’s going to sue them.

speaker: BUSH
text: People don’t dare — medical practitioners, to help somebody along the highway that are hurt because they’re afraid that some lawyer’s going to come along and get a big lawsuit.

speaker: BUSH
text: So you can’t blame the practitioners for the health problem.

speaker: BUSH
text: And my program is this.

speaker: BUSH
text: Keep the government as far out of it as possible, make insurance available to the poorest of the poor, through vouchers, next range in the income bracket, through tax credits, and get on about the business of pooling insurance.

speaker: BUSH
text: A great big company can buy — Ross has got a good-sized company, been very successful.

speaker: BUSH
text: He can buy insurance cheaper than Mom and Pop’s store on the corner.

speaker: BUSH
text: But if those Mom and Pop stores all get together and pool, they too can bring the cost of insurance down.

speaker: BUSH
text: So I want to keep the quality of health care.

speaker: BUSH
text: That means keep government out of it.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want to do — I don’t like this idea of these boards.

speaker: BUSH
text: It all sounds to me like you’re going to have some government setting price.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want competition and I want to pool the insurance and take care of it that way and have — oh, here’s the other point.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think medical care should go with the person.

speaker: BUSH
text: If you leave a business, I think your insurance should go with you to some other business.

speaker: BUSH
text: You shouldn’t be worrying if you get a new job as to whether that’s gonna — and part of our plan is to make it what they call portable — big word, but that means if you’re working for the Jones Company and you go to the Smith Company, your insurance goes with you.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think it’s a good program.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m really excited about getting it done, too.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot.

speaker: PEROT
text: We have the most expensive health care system in the world.

speaker: PEROT
text: Twelve percent of our gross national product goes to health care.

speaker: PEROT
text: Our industrial competitors, who are beating us in competition, spend less and have better health care.

speaker: PEROT
text: Japan spends a little over 6% of its gross national product.

speaker: PEROT
text: Germany spends 8%.

speaker: PEROT
text: It’s fascinating.

speaker: PEROT
text: You’ve bought a front row box seat and you’re not happy with your health care and you’re saying tonight we’ve got bad health care but very expensive health care.

speaker: PEROT
text: Folks, here’s why.

speaker: PEROT
text: Go home and look in the mirror.

speaker: PEROT
text: You own this country but you have no voice in it the way it’s organized now, and if you want to have a high risk experience, comparable to bungee jumping, go into Congress some time when they’re working on this kind of legislation, when the lobbyists are running up and down the halls.

speaker: PEROT
text: Wear your safety toe shoes when you go.

speaker: PEROT
text: And as a private citizen, believe me, you are looked on as a major nuisance.

speaker: PEROT
text: The facts are you now have a government that comes at you.

speaker: PEROT
text: You’re supposed to have a government that comes from you.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, there are all kinds of good ideas, brilliant ideas, terrific ideas on health care.

speaker: PEROT
text: None of them ever get implemented because — let me give you an example.

speaker: PEROT
text: A senator runs every 6 years.

speaker: PEROT
text: He’s got to raise 20,000 bucks a week to have enough money to run.

speaker: PEROT
text: Who’s he gonna listen to — us or the folks running up and down the aisles with money, the lobbyists, the PAC money?

speaker: PEROT
text: He listens to them.

speaker: PEROT
text: Who do they represent?

speaker: PEROT
text: Health care industry.

speaker: PEROT
text: Not us.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, you’ve got to have a government that comes from you again.

speaker: PEROT
text: You’ve got to reassert your ownership in this country and you’ve got to completely reform our government.

speaker: PEROT
text: And at that point they’ll just be like apples falling out of a tree.

speaker: PEROT
text: The programs will be good because the elected officials will be listening to — I said the other night I was all ears and I would listen to any good idea.

speaker: PEROT
text: I think we ought to do plastic surgery on a lot of these guys so that they’re all ears, too, and listen to you.

speaker: PEROT
text: Then you get what you want, and shouldn’t you?

speaker: PEROT
text: You paid for it.

speaker: PEROT
text: Why shouldn’t you get what you want, as opposed to what some lobbyist cuts a deal, writes a little piece in the law and he goes through.

speaker: PEROT
text: That’s the way the game’s played now.

speaker: PEROT
text: Till you change it you’re gonna be unhappy.

speaker: PEROT
text: SIMPSON : You wanted one brief point in there.

speaker: CLINTON
text: One brief point.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We have elections so people can make decisions about this.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The point I want to make to you is, a bipartisan commission reviewed my plan and the Bush plan and there were as many Republicans as Democratic health care experts on it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: They concluded that my plan would cover everybody and his would leave 27 million behind by the year 2000 and that my plan in the next 12 years would save $2.

speaker: CLINTON
text: 2 trillion in public and private money to reinvest in this economy and the average family would save $1200 a year under the plan that I offered without any erosion in the quality of health care So I ask you to look at that.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And you have to vote for somebody with a plan.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That’s what you have elections for.

speaker: CLINTON
text: If people would say, well, he got elected to do this and then the Congress says, okay, I’m going to do it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That’s what the election was about.

speaker: CLINTON
text: END of first half of 1992 Debate 2 October 15, 1992 Second Half Debate Transcript October 15, 1992 The Second Clinton-Bush-Perot Presidential Debate This is the second half of the transcript of the Richmond debate.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The October 15th “town hall” format debate was moderated by Carole Simpson.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The length of this printed transcript is approximately 20 pages.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Brief, Governor Clinton.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: We have a question right here.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Yes.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: How has the national debt personally affected each of your lives?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: And if it hasn’t, how can you honestly find a cure for the economic problems of the common people if you have no experience in what’s ailing them?

speaker: PEROT
text: May I answer that?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Well, Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot — yes, of course.

speaker: PEROT
text: Who do you want to start with?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: My question is for each of you, so-

speaker: PEROT
text: It caused me to disrupt my private life and my business to get involved in this activity.

speaker: PEROT
text: That’s how much I care about it.

speaker: PEROT
text: And believe me, if you knew my family and if you knew the private life I have, you would agree in a minute that that’s a whole lot more fun than getting involved in politics.

speaker: PEROT
text: But I have lived the American dream.

speaker: PEROT
text: I came from very modest background.

speaker: PEROT
text: Nobody’s been luckier than I’ve been, all the way across the spectrum, and the greatest riches of all are my wife and children.

speaker: PEROT
text: That’s true of any family.

speaker: PEROT
text: But I want all the children — I want these young people up here to be able to start with nothing but an idea like I did and build a business.

speaker: PEROT
text: But they’ve got to have a strong basic economy and if you’re in debt, it’s like having a ball and chain around you.

speaker: PEROT
text: I just figure, as lucky as I’ve been, I owe it to them and I owe it to the future generations and on a very personal basis, I owe it to my children and grandchildren.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you, Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: President.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, I think the national debt affects everybody.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: You personally.

speaker: BUSH
text: Obviously it has a lot to do with interest rates —

speaker: SIMPSON
text: She’s saying, “you personally”

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: You, on a personal basis — how has it affected you?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Has it affected you personally?

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m sure it has.

speaker: BUSH
text: I love my grandchildren —

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: How?

speaker: BUSH
text: I want to think that they’re going to be able to afford an education.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think that that’s an important part of being a parent.

speaker: BUSH
text: If the question — maybe I — get it wrong.

speaker: BUSH
text: Are you suggesting that if somebody has means that the national debt doesn’t affect them?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: What I’m saying is —

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m not sure I get — help me with the question and I’ll try to answer it.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Well, I’ve had friends that have been laid off from jobs.

speaker: BUSH
text: Yeah.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: I know people who cannot afford to pay the mortgage on their homes, their car payment.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: I have personal problems with the national debt.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: But how has it affected you and if you have no experience in it, how can you help us, if you don’t know what we’re feeling?

speaker: SIMPSON
text: I think she means more the recession — the economic problems today the country faces rather than the deficit.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, listen, you ought to be in the White House for a day and hear what I hear and see what I see and read the mail I read and touch the people that I touch from time to time.

speaker: BUSH
text: I was in the Lomax AME Church.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s a black church just outside of Washington, DC.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I read in the bulletin about teenage pregnancies, about the difficulties that families are having to make ends meet.

speaker: BUSH
text: I talk to parents.

speaker: BUSH
text: I mean, you’ve got to care.

speaker: BUSH
text: Everybody cares if people aren’t doing well.

speaker: BUSH
text: But I don’t think it’s fair to say, you haven’t had cancer.

speaker: BUSH
text: Therefore, you don’t know what’s it like.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t think it’s fair to say, you know, whatever it is, that if you haven’t been hit by it personally.

speaker: BUSH
text: But everybody’s affected by the debt because of the tremendous interest that goes into paying on that debt everything’s more expensive.

speaker: BUSH
text: Everything comes out of your pocket and my pocket.

speaker: BUSH
text: So it’s that.

speaker: BUSH
text: But I think in terms of the recession, of course you feel it when you’re president of the US.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that’s why I’m trying to do something about it by stimulating the export, vesting more, better education systems.

speaker: BUSH
text: Thank you.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m glad you clarified it.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Governor Clinton.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Tell me how it’s affected you again.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Um —

speaker: CLINTON
text: You know people who’ve lost their jobs and lost their homes?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Well, yeah, uh-huh.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Well, I’ve been governor of a small state for 12 years.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ll tell you how it’s affected me.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Every year Congress and the president sign laws that make us do more things and gives us less money to do it with.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I see people in my state, middle class people — their taxes have gone up in Washington and their services have gone down while the wealthy have gotten tax cuts.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I have seen what’s happened in this last 4 years when — in my state, when people lose their jobs there’s a good chance I’ll know them by their names.

speaker: CLINTON
text: When a factory closes, I know the people who ran it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: When the businesses go bankrupt, I know them.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And I’ve been out here for 13 months meeting in meetings just like this ever since October, with people like you all over America, people that have lost their jobs, lost their livelihood, lost their health insurance.

speaker: CLINTON
text: What I want you to understand is the national debt is not the only cause of that.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It is because America has not invested in its people.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It is because we have not grown.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It is because we’ve had 12 years of trickle down economics.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We’ve gone from first to twelfth in the world in wages.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We’ve had 4 years where we’ve produced no private sector jobs.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Most people are working harder for less money than they were making ten years ago.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It is because we are in the grip of a failed economic theory.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And this decision you’re about to make better be about what kind of economic theory you want, not just people saying I’m going to go fix it but what are we going to do?

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think we have to do is invest in American jobs, American education, control American health care costs and bring the American people together again.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Thank you.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you, Governor Clinton.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: We are a little more than halfway through this program and I’m glad we’re getting the diversity of questions that we are, and I don’t want to forget these folks on the wings over here so let’s go over here.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Do you have a question?

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: Yes, I do.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: My name is Ben Smith.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: I work in the financial field, counseling retirees, and I’m personally concerned about three major areas.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: One is the Social Security Administration or trust fund is projected to be insolvent by the year 2036.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: And we funded the trust fund with IOUs in the form of Treasury bonds.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: The Pension Guarantee Fund, which backs up our private retirement plans for retirees, is projected to be bankrupt by the year 2026, not to mention the cutbacks by private companies.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: And Medicare is projected to be bankrupt maybe as soon as 1997.

speaker: AUDIENCE QUESTION
text: And I would like from each of you a specific response as to what you intend to do for retirees relative to these issues, not generalities but specifics because I think they’re very disturbing issues.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: President Bush, may we start with you?

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, the Social Security — you’re an expert and I could, I’m sure, learn from you the details of the Pension Guarantee Fund and the Social Security Fund.

speaker: BUSH
text: The Social Security system was fixed about 5 years, and I think it’s projected out to be sound beyond that.

speaker: BUSH
text: So at least we have time to work with it.

speaker: BUSH
text: But on all of these things, a sound economy is the only way to get it going.

speaker: BUSH
text: Growth in the economy is gonna add to the overall prosperity and wealth.

speaker: BUSH
text: I can’t give you a specific answer on Pension Guarantee Fund.

speaker: BUSH
text: All I know is that we have firm government credit to guarantee the pensions.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that is very important.

speaker: BUSH
text: But it’s — the full faith and credit of the US, in spite of our difficulties, is still pretty good.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s still the most respected credit.

speaker: BUSH
text: So I would simply say, as these dates get close, you’re going to have to reorganize and refix as we did with the Social Security Fund.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I think that’s the only answer.

speaker: BUSH
text: But the more immediate answer is to do what this lady was suggesting we do, and that is to get this deficit down and get on without adding to the woes, and then restructure.

speaker: BUSH
text: One thing I’ve called for that has been stymied, and I’ll keep on working for it, is a whole financial reform legislation.

speaker: BUSH
text: It is absolutely essential in terms of bringing our banking system and credit system into the new age instead of having it living back in the dark ages.

speaker: BUSH
text: And it’s a big fight.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I don’t want to give my friend Ross another shot at me here but I am fighting with the Congress to get this through.

speaker: BUSH
text: And you can’t just go up and say I’m going to fix it.

speaker: BUSH
text: You’ve got some pretty strong-willed guys up there that argue with you.

speaker: BUSH
text: But that’s what the election’s about.

speaker: BUSH
text: I agree with the governor.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what the election’s about.

speaker: BUSH
text: And sound fiscal policy is the best answer, I think, to all the three problems you mentioned.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Thank you.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot.

speaker: PEROT
text: On the broad issue here, when you’re trying to solve a problem, you get the best plans.

speaker: PEROT
text: You have a raging debate about those plans.

speaker: PEROT
text: Then out of that debate, with leadership, comes consensus.

speaker: PEROT
text: Then, if the plans are huge and complex like health care, I would urge you to implement pilot programs.

speaker: PEROT
text: Like the old carpenter says measure twice, cut once.

speaker: PEROT
text: Let’s make sure this thing’s as good as we all think it is at the end of the meeting.

speaker: PEROT
text: Then finally, our government passes laws and freezes the plan in concrete.

speaker: PEROT
text: Anybody that’s ever built a successful business will tell you you optimize, optimize, optimize after you’ve put something into effect.

speaker: PEROT
text: The reason Medicare and Medicaid are a mess is we froze them.

speaker: PEROT
text: Everybody knows how to fix them.

speaker: PEROT
text: There are people all over the federal government, if they could just touch it with a screwdriver, could fix it.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, back over here.

speaker: PEROT
text: See, we’ve got a $4 trillion debt and only in America would you have $2.

speaker: PEROT
text: 8 trillion of it or 70% of it financed 5 years or less.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, that’s another thing for you to think about when you go home tonight.

speaker: PEROT
text: You don’t finance long-term debt with short-term money.

speaker: PEROT
text: Why did our government do it?

speaker: PEROT
text: To get the interest rates down.

speaker: PEROT
text: A 1% increase in interest rates in that $2.

speaker: PEROT
text: 8 trillion is $28 billion a year.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, when you look at what Germany pays for money and what we don’t pay for money, you realize there’s quite a spread, right, and you realize this is a temporary thing and there’s going to be another sucking sound that runs our deficit through the roof.

speaker: PEROT
text: You know, and everybody’s ducking it so I’m gonna say it, that we are not letting that surplus stay in the bank.

speaker: PEROT
text: We are not investing that surplus like a pension fund.

speaker: PEROT
text: We are spending that surplus to make the deficit look smaller to you than it really is.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, that — put you in jail in corporate America if you kept books that way but in government it’s just kind of the way things are.

speaker: PEROT
text: That’s because it comes at you, not from you.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now then, that money needs to be — they don’t even pay interest on it.

speaker: PEROT
text: They just write a note for the interest.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Mr.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: Perot, can you wrap it up?

speaker: PEROT
text: Do you want to fix the problem or sound-bite it?

speaker: PEROT
text: I understand the importance of time but see, here’s how we get to this mess we’re in.

speaker: SIMPSON
text: But we’ve got to be fair.

speaker: PEROT
text: This is just 1 of 1000.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now then, to nail it, there’s one way out — a growing, expanding job base.

speaker: PEROT
text: A growing, expanding job base to generate the funds and the tax revenues to pay off the mess and rebuild America.

speaker: PEROT
